Anisotropy from a dipole selection rule and 2D confinement of the exciton envelope are distinct statements... GW+BSE is not "beyond the scope". Refs. 12, 13 and 48 have already done it.

Measure polarized transmission (and ideally retardance) on a polished, oriented thin plate to obtain α_ab(λ), α_c(λ) and Δn directly in the visible.

A linear ln α from 1 to 3.35 eV implies a characteristic energy of order 1 eV, which is not an Urbach tail in the usual sense.
The definition also differs from how transparency is defined for the comparison materials in Fig. 3: rutile, calcite and LiNbO3 have α of order 10⁻² to 10⁰ cm⁻¹ there.
The extraction of ε_ab and ε_c from a uniaxial crystal is not justified... This suggests leakage of ε_ab into the "c-axis" spectrum.
The Tauc extraction (Fig. S5) is fitted over about 0.05 eV on an excitonic line shape.
the side faces in Fig. S1 and Fig. 1b look visibly stepped and textured rather than optically flat... Surface roughness ... reduce and distort the apparent ε2 peak
The "highest reported to date" comparison is not like-for-like. |Δn|max = 3.67 and |Δk|max = 5.21 are resonant values at a strong exciton, where k_ab ≈ 5.
It attributes "direct bandgap of about 3.71 eV" to Ref. 15, which reports about 3.5 eV.
The "forbidden for c-polarization" statement is argued from atomic-orbital parity, not from the little group at L or from computed momentum matrix elements.
The "transparency across the entire visible spectrum" and "without optical loss" claims contradict the paper's own data... and the crystals are black (Fig. 1b).
